chapters.title: Blessing: Berakhah and the Blessing vs blessings
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible, blessing is God's life-giving favour, given to one family so that it can flow to all the families of the earth
chapters.trueMeaning: God's life-giving favour, received in order to be passed on
chapters.nutshell: Today “blessed” often means “I got something good”: a car, a job, a holiday. In Hebrew, *barakh* is God filling people with life and fruitfulness, and people answering by “blessing” (praising) God. English “blessed” also hides a second word, *ashrei* (Greek *makarios*), “how fortunate, on the right path”. Above all, Scripture speaks of **the Blessing** promised to Abraham, a blessing with a purpose: “you will be a blessing… in you all the families of the earth will be blessed.”
chapters.bigIdea: God blesses his people with life so that they become a blessing; the Blessing of Abraham reaches the nations through the Messiah.
skeleton: We often hear “blessed” as “I received good things”
Barakh and berakhah: God fills creation with life; people bless God and one another
English “blessed” hides two words: barukh (blessed by God, or praised) and ashrei / makarios (fortunate, flourishing)
The Blessing: Abraham is blessed in order to be a blessing to all the families of the earth
Blessings (plural) are gifts along the way; Jesus' Beatitudes overturn the prosperity reading
Jewish practice blesses God for food and life, and Jesus “blessed and broke” the bread

p: Scroll through social media and you will see **#blessed** under a new house, a promotion or a beach holiday. In everyday speech, “blessed” has come to mean “I have received good things”, and “God bless you” sounds like a kind wish for comfort and success.

The Bible does speak of good gifts. But its words for blessing are bigger and more purposeful. God's first blessing is life itself; people “bless” God as well as receive blessing; and one great Blessing is given to Abraham's family **so that it can flow outward** to the whole world.

sections.h: Barakh and berakhah: life that overflows
p: The Hebrew verb *barakh* (בָּרַךְ), used mostly in its intensive form *berakh*, means “to bless”; the noun is *berakhah* (בְּרָכָה), “a blessing”. The same letters spell *berekh* (בֶּרֶךְ), “knee”, and *berekhah* (בְּרֵכָה), “pool”. Many teachers link blessing with kneeling or with a pool of refreshing water, but whether the words share an origin is **debated**; treat it as a picture, not a proof.

The first blessing in the Bible is life: God blessed the sea creatures and the birds, and then the man and the woman, saying, “**Be fruitful and multiply**” (Genesis 1:22, 28). To be blessed is to be filled with God's power for life, growth and fruitfulness.

Blessing moves in more than one direction. God blesses people. People **bless God**: “Bless the LORD, O my soul” (Psalm 103:1), meaning praise and thank him, perhaps on bended knee. People bless one another: Isaac blesses Jacob (Genesis 27), Jacob lays his hands on Joseph's sons (Genesis 48:14), and in the fields Boaz's workers greet him, “**The LORD bless you**” (Ruth 2:4). Jesus took children in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them (Mark 10:16).

sections.h: Barukh and ashrei: two kinds of “blessed”
p: English uses one word, “blessed”, for two different Hebrew ideas. *Barukh* (בָּרוּךְ) means “blessed” in the sense of **endowed with God's favour** (“Blessed be Abram by God Most High”, Genesis 14:19), or, when said of God, “**praised**” (“Blessed be the LORD”, Genesis 24:27). The Greek translators normally used *eulogeō*, “to speak well of”, and *eulogia*, “blessing”.

*Ashrei* (אַשְׁרֵי) is a different word. “**Blessed is the man** who walks not in the counsel of the wicked” (Psalm 1:1) means “**how fortunate**, how well it goes with” the person who walks on the right path. The Greek for *ashrei* is *makarios*, the word Jesus uses in the Beatitudes: “**Blessed are the poor in spirit**” (Matthew 5:3). *Ashrei* is never said of God; it describes a flourishing human life. Some translations keep the two apart: the Tamil Bible says *pākkiyavān* (“fortunate one”) for *ashrei* and *makarios*, and a form of *āsīrvathi* for *barukh*.

sections.h: The Blessing: blessed to be a blessing
p: In Genesis 12:1–3 God calls Abram: “I will bless you and make your name great, and **be a blessing**… and in you **all the families of the earth** shall be blessed.” The Hebrew *veh'yeh berakhah* is an imperative, “and be a blessing!”, which many read as purpose: “so that you will be a blessing”. The promise is repeated to Abraham (18:18; 22:18), Isaac (26:4) and Jacob (28:14). This is not a pile of gifts but **one covenant Blessing with a mission**.

The New Testament says this Blessing reaches the nations through the Messiah. Peter tells the crowd that God sent his servant “**to bless you** by turning every one of you from your wickedness” (Acts 3:25–26). Paul says the Scripture “preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham” and that in Christ “**the blessing of Abraham** might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith” (Galatians 3:8–9, 14). God “has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3).

Scripture also speaks of **blessings** in the plural: rain in its season, harvest, children, safety and peace, the covenant blessings of Deuteronomy 28:1–14. “The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it” (Proverbs 10:22). Through Malachi God promises to “pour down for you a blessing” on a faithful nation (Malachi 3:10). These gifts are real and good, and Israel thanked God for them.

Some teaching reads Deuteronomy 28 or 3 John 2 (“I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health”) as a promise that every faithful believer will be wealthy. To be fair, it rightly says God cares about bodies and daily bread. But Deuteronomy 28 is addressed to the **nation** under the Sinai covenant, and 3 John 2 is a normal letter greeting. Jesus turns the easy equation upside down: “**Blessed are you who are poor… Blessed are you who mourn**” and “Woe to you who are rich” (Luke 6:20–26; Matthew 5:3–12). Blessing flows outward; it is not for hoarding.

sections.h: Blessing at the table and in Jesus' hands
p: Jewish prayer is built on the *berakhah*: “*Barukh attah Adonai, Eloheinu, melekh ha-olam*… Blessed are you, LORD our God, King of the universe, who…”. The fixed wording was standardised in the **rabbinic period**, after the New Testament, but the habit is ancient: “You shall eat and be full, and you shall **bless the LORD** your God” (Deuteronomy 8:10). The Talmud records a teaching that one should say a hundred blessings each day (Menachot 43b); it shows the ideal of a life full of thanks. Over bread the blessing ends “*ha-motzi lechem min ha-aretz*”, “who brings forth bread from the earth”, and over wine “who creates the fruit of the vine”. Note who is blessed: **God**, for the food. Each blessing is answered with “Amen”.

So when Jesus “looked up to heaven and **said a blessing** and broke the loaves” (Mark 6:41; also 14:22; Luke 24:30), he was thanking his Father in the Jewish way. The priestly blessing, *birkat kohanim*, “The LORD bless you and keep you…” (Numbers 6:24–26), was found on two tiny silver scrolls at **Ketef Hinnom** in Jerusalem, usually dated to around 600 BC (some scholars date them later), among the oldest known fragments of biblical text. Many Jewish parents also bless their children on Friday evening with this blessing, a custom that developed **later**.

chapters.title: Blessing and Curse: Life and Death Set Before You
chapters.subtitle: A biblical curse is not a magic spell but the loss of blessing; God set life and death before Israel, and in the Messiah the curse is carried away
chapters.trueMeaning: Being cut off from blessing, made light and empty instead of full of life
chapters.nutshell: Many people fear curses as hidden spells that can strike at any time. Hebrew has several words for curse: *arar* (to bind or ban from blessing), *qalal* (to make light, treat with contempt), *alah* (the oath-curse of a covenant) and *cherem* (devoted to destruction). In the Bible, blessings and curses are mainly the two sides of God's covenant: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse; therefore choose life.” The Messiah “became a curse for us” so that one day “there will no longer be any curse”.
chapters.bigIdea: Curse is life drained away by turning from God; the covenant sets this choice before us, and Christ bore the curse so that the Blessing could come.
skeleton: We often picture curses as magic spells to be feared
Hebrew uses several words: arar, qalal, alah, cherem; Greek katara and anathema
Blessing and curse are the sanctions of the covenant, set before Israel at Gerizim and Ebal
Words are not automatic power: a causeless curse does not land, and Balaam could only bless
Christ became a curse for us; believers bless those who curse them
Popular fears such as “generational curses” are tested against the whole of Scripture

p: In many cultures, including much of South Asia and Africa, people fear curses: a word spoken in anger, an evil eye, a charm buried near a house. Some Christians worry about curses passed down through families, or think that missing a tithe brings a curse on their finances.

The Bible takes curse seriously, but it means something different. A biblical curse is mainly the **opposite of blessing**: life drained away, fruitfulness lost, distance from God. And it is not a power anyone can switch on; it sits inside God's covenant and under God's rule.

*Arar* (אָרַר) is the strongest: to **bind, ban, cut off from blessing**. “**Cursed** is the ground because of you” (Genesis 3:17; also 3:14; 4:11). The twelve declarations of Deuteronomy 27:15–26 each begin *arur*, “cursed is the one who…”.

*Qalal* (קָלַל) means to be **light, slight**, so to **treat with contempt**. It is the opposite of *kaved*, “heavy”, from which comes *kavod*, “glory, honour”. Honouring someone gives them weight; despising them makes them light. Genesis 12:3 uses both words in one verse: “I will bless those who bless you, and the one who **treats you lightly** (*qalal*) I will **curse** (*arar*).” The noun *qelalah*, “curse”, comes from this root (Deuteronomy 30:19).

*Alah* (אָלָה) is the **oath-curse** attached to a covenant: you swear loyalty and call down a penalty on yourself if you break it (Deuteronomy 29:12, 19–21; Numbers 5:21). *Cherem* (חֵרֶם) is something **devoted** to God, often for destruction, as at Jericho (Joshua 6:17). In Greek, *katara* is “curse”, *epikataratos* “cursed” (Galatians 3:10, 13), and *anathema*, the Septuagint's word for *cherem*, “accursed, devoted” (Galatians 1:8–9; Romans 9:3).

sections.h: Covenant sanctions: life and death set before you
p: In the Bible, blessings and curses belong mainly to the **covenant**. Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27–28 end the Sinai covenant with blessings for faithfulness and curses for unfaithfulness: drought, failed harvests, disease, defeat and, at the end, **exile** from the land. Ancient Near Eastern treaties, such as Hittite and Assyrian vassal treaties, also ended with lists of blessings and curses, and scholars often note the similar shape; the details of the comparison are debated.

Moses told Israel to proclaim the blessing on **Mount Gerizim** and the curse on **Mount Ebal**, the two mountains that face each other above **Shechem** (Deuteronomy 11:26–29; 27:11–13). Joshua carried it out, reading “all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse” (Joshua 8:30–35). The heart of it is a choice: “I have set before you **life and death, blessing and curse**. Therefore **choose life**… loving the LORD your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life” (Deuteronomy 30:15–20).

sections.h: Not magic: the causeless curse and Balaam
p: Biblical cursing is not a spell with automatic power. “Like a sparrow in its flitting, like a swallow in its flying, **a curse that is causeless does not alight**” (Proverbs 26:2). Words matter, but they do not overrule God.

The clearest story is **Balaam**, a famous diviner hired by the king of Moab to curse Israel (Numbers 22–24). Three times he tried, and three times he could only bless: “How can I curse whom God has not cursed?” (23:8). Moses later said, “the LORD your God **turned the curse into a blessing** for you, because the LORD your God loved you” (Deuteronomy 23:5).

Even the first curse carries hope. The ground was cursed after Eden (Genesis 3:17), and when Noah was born his father said, “this one shall bring us **relief** from our work… out of the ground that the LORD has cursed” (Genesis 5:29). The name *Noach* sounds like the word for relief or comfort.

Paul writes that “all who rely on works of the law are under a curse” (Galatians 3:10), and then: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by **becoming a curse for us**, for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (Galatians 3:13, quoting Deuteronomy 21:23). The Messiah entered the place of curse, the exile and death that the covenant warned of, so that “the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles” (3:14). The story ends with the curse gone: “**No longer will there be anything accursed**” (Revelation 22:3; compare Zechariah 14:11).

So Jesus' followers answer curse with blessing: “**Bless those who curse you**, pray for those who abuse you” (Luke 6:28; Romans 12:14; 1 Peter 3:9). James notes how strange it is that “from the same mouth come blessing and cursing” (James 3:9–10). The reversal Balaam experienced becomes the way of life of God's people.

**Generational curses.** Exodus 20:5–6 says God visits iniquity “to the third and fourth generation of those who **hate me**”, but shows steadfast love “to **thousands** of those who love me”. The point is the contrast: judgment is limited, love is vast. Families do pass on patterns of sin and their consequences. But Scripture also insists that each person is judged for their own sin: “The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18:20; Jeremiah 31:29–30; Deuteronomy 24:16). Jesus refused to blame a man's blindness on his parents (John 9:2–3).

**Tithing curses.** In Malachi 3:9 the whole nation is “cursed with a curse” for robbing God of tithes meant for the Temple storehouse, the Levites and the poor; it is a covenant word to Israel, not a hidden spell on individual Christians. **The fig tree** that Jesus cursed (Mark 11:12–25) surrounds his action in the Temple; many interpreters read it as a **prophetic sign** about a Temple that had leaves but no fruit, not as a lesson in cursing.
